---
title: "Exporting results"
---

A scenario grid usually ends up in a report, a costing spreadsheet, or a colleague's R
session. The frame `run_scenarios` returns does not travel as it stands. Two of its columns
hold NumPy arrays rather than numbers. The scalars and the trajectories need separate files.

The grid is the same five arms built in [A scenario grid](scenario-grid.qmd), rebuilt from
the same district dictionary.

```{python}
import pathlib

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from estimint import run_scenarios, preload_models
from estimint.scenarios import Scenario, EirTarget

district = dict(
    res_use=0.30, Q0=0.85, phi=0.80, seasonal=0.0, irs=0.0,
    py_only=0.70, routine=0.0,
    eir_target=EirTarget(0.45, "prevalence"),
)

grid = [
    Scenario(name="Withdraw", **district),
    Scenario(name="Pyrethroid-only", itn_future=0.70,
             net_type_future="pyrethroid_only", **district),
    Scenario(name="PBO", itn_future=0.70,
             net_type_future="pyrethroid_pbo", **district),
    Scenario(name="Pyrrole", itn_future=0.70,
             net_type_future="pyrethroid_pyrrole", **district),
    Scenario(name="PBO + IRS + LSM", itn_future=0.70,
             net_type_future="pyrethroid_pbo", irs_future=0.60, lsm=0.30, **district),
]

res = run_scenarios(grid)
```

## An output directory

`pathlib` is Python's path library. A `Path` is an object rather than a string, one that
composes with `/` and can make its own directory.

```{python}
outputs = pathlib.Path("outputs")
outputs.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

outputs.resolve()
```

`exist_ok=True` makes the call idempotent, so the cell can be re-run without raising on the
second pass. Paths are resolved relative to the working directory of the session, not to the
file the code sits in. Under Quarto the working directory is the project root, so `outputs/`
lands at the top of the project.

## The scalar summary

Twenty-one of the twenty-three columns are scalars. Those are the ones that belong in a
spreadsheet. Drop the other two first.

```{python}
summary = res.drop(columns=["prevalence", "cases"])
summary.to_csv(outputs / "summary.csv", index=False)

pd.read_csv(outputs / "summary.csv")[
    ["name", "net_future", "dn0_future", "eir_baseline", "prev_endline", "cases_endline"]
]
```

`index=False` suppresses pandas' row numbers, which are an artefact of the frame and not
data. Reading the file straight back is worth the two seconds. It is the only way to find
out that a column expected to be numeric has come back as text.

## Array columns in a CSV

`to_csv` does not refuse an array column. It writes the array's text representation into the
cell, which is the string that printing the array would produce, brackets and line breaks
included.

```{python}
res.to_csv(outputs / "summary-broken.csv", index=False)

broken = pd.read_csv(outputs / "summary-broken.csv")
cell = broken.loc[0, "prevalence"]

type(cell), len(cell), cell[:60]
```

What comes back is a single string some 1,700 characters long, not 157 numbers. The file is
valid CSV and opens in any spreadsheet, so no error is raised. The column is text from then
on. Any analysis downstream either fails on it or silently skips it. In R, `read_csv` will
type it as `chr` and move on.

The array is not truncated here. NumPy only elides long arrays above a thousand elements,
and 157 is below the threshold, so the numbers are all present, embedded in a string with
newlines in it. Recovering them requires parsing that string. Drop the array columns before
writing instead.

```{python}
(outputs / "summary-broken.csv").unlink()
```

## Tidy format

The trajectories want their own file in long form, one row per scenario per timestep. That
is the shape `ggplot2` and `dplyr` expect. Recover the time grid from the emulator, then
stack the arrays.

```{python}
_, artifacts = preload_models()
cfg = artifacts["prevalence"].preprocessing_config

n_steps = cfg["n_steps"]
abs_t = cfg["model_start_day"] + cfg["window_size"] * np.arange(n_steps)
years = (abs_t - cfg["intervention_day"]) / 365

trajectories = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "name": np.repeat(res["name"].to_numpy(), n_steps),
        "day": np.tile(abs_t, len(res)),
        "years": np.tile(years, len(res)),
        "prevalence": np.concatenate(res["prevalence"].to_list()),
        "cases": np.concatenate(res["cases"].to_list()),
    }
)

trajectories.shape
```

`np.repeat` gives each scenario name 157 consecutive rows; `np.tile` repeats the time grid
once per scenario; `np.concatenate` on the list of arrays flattens them in the same order.
Five scenarios of 157 windows is 785 rows.

```{python}
trajectories.head()
```

Keeping both `day` and `years` costs one column and saves an argument later. `day` is the
model's own clock and is what you would join on. `years` is centred on the campaign and is
what you would plot against.

```{python}
trajectories.to_csv(outputs / "trajectories.csv", index=False)

sorted(p.name for p in outputs.iterdir())
```

## Reading the files in R

Both files are plain CSV with a header row. Nothing about them is Python-specific.

```r
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

summary <- read_csv("outputs/summary.csv")
traj <- read_csv("outputs/trajectories.csv")

summary |>
  select(name, net_future, dn0_future, prev_endline, cases_endline) |>
  arrange(prev_endline)

ggplot(traj, aes(x = years, y = prevalence, colour = name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    x = "Years since campaign",
    y = "Prevalence (under 5)",
    colour = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

`read_csv` types the columns from the data, so `name` comes through as a character vector
and everything else as a double. The `years` column puts the campaign at zero, which makes
`geom_vline(xintercept = 0)` the R equivalent of the dashed campaign rule on the matplotlib
figures.

For a longer-lived pipeline, prefer Parquet over CSV, with `trajectories.to_parquet()` on
the Python side and `arrow::read_parquet()` on the R side. It preserves dtypes exactly, the
files are smaller, and a number cannot come back as text.
